label: Can't make it
rationale: The stock reasons for saying no or heading off: something on, an early start, already booked, a prior engagement.
mixUps: All use aru or hairu, never motsu. youji ga atte is the vague errand excuse, yotei haitteru says the day is taken, senyaku ga atte is the politer 'prior engagement'; asa hayai kara makes the morning the subject. Something 'comes up' as youji ga dekita or yotei ga haitta, not okita.

targets.trap: English 'have' leads to motsu, but having plans or errands is aru (youji ga aru). And 'something came up' is youji ga dekita, not kita or okita.
targets.use: The vague, polite reason for saying no or leaving: chotto youji ga atte..., left unfinished so the listener hears 'so I can't'. Nobody asks what the youji is. When something comes up, the verb is dekiru: kyuu ni youji ga dekichatte (something came up).

example.ja: 明日はちょっと用事あって…
example.english: Tomorrow I've got something on, so...

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa chotto youji ga aru n desu ga...
examplePolite.ja: 明日はちょっと用事があるんですが…
examplePolite.english: I've got something on tomorrow, I'm afraid...

partners: kaeri (getting home: kyou kaeri hayai ne)
targets.use: The standard reason to leave or go to bed early: ashita asa hayai kara, mou neru ne. ga is nearly always dropped, and ashita hayai kara alone is common too. Said about someone's routine, asa hayai ne means they're up early.
targets.notes: The opposite is asa ga osoi (a late start), and asa yowai means you're not a morning person. ashita hayaku okinakya (I have to get up early) works just as well.

example.romaji: ashita asa hayai kara, mou neru ne.
example.ja: 明日朝早いから、もう寝るね。
example.english: I've got an early start tomorrow, so I'm off to bed.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa asa ga hayai node, mou nemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は朝が早いので、もう寝ますね。
examplePolite.english: I've got an early start tomorrow, so I'll go to bed now.

targets.verbSense: go in, enter; get put into something
targets.trap: 'Something came up' is kyuu ni youji ga dekita or kyuu ni yotei ga haitta, not okita (that sounds like an accident). Plain 'I have plans' is yotei ga aru, never yotei o motteru; haitteru adds that the day is already taken.
targets.use: Mostly as haitteru (is booked) or haitta (got booked): sono hi wa mou yotei haitteru. A sudden clash is kyuu ni yotei haitchatte.
targets.notes: Transitive partner: yotei o ireru (book something in).

example.ja: 明日はもう予定入ってる

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa mou yotei ga haittemasu
examplePolite.ja: 明日はもう予定が入ってます

targets.use: The polite way to turn down an invitation for a particular day: sumimasen, sono hi wa sen'yaku ga atte..., left trailing, since a flat ...kara sounds like an excuse. Friends say it too (gomen, sen'yaku aru n da) when the plan is with someone else; yotei aru is vaguer.
targets.notes: Same trailing shape as youji ga atte...: the 'so I can't' is left unsaid.

example.romaji: gomen, sono hi wa senyaku ga atte...
example.ja: ごめん、その日は先約があって…
example.english: Sorry, I've already got plans that day...

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sono hi wa senyaku ga aru n desu ga...
examplePolite.ja: すみません、その日は先約があるんですが…
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I already have plans that day...

not suit someone, can't make it (a time)
